jokes.text: The Friends guest is 'George McAtee,' a character actor who 'played the janitor with the shaky leg on episode 14.'
jokes.setup: The network exec excitedly asks which Friends star Jon Stewart will have on the show.

jokes.explanation: Classic Larry Sanders insider comedy — the specificity of 'the janitor with the shaky leg on episode 14' is what sells it. Artie's deadpan delivery implies total institutional pride in booking a nobody. Strong character integration (only a pompous, oblivious producer would say this) and economical setup/payoff. Earns its laughs through industry-specific wit rather than cheap shots.

jokes.text: John Tesh as musician, journalist, AND sportscaster: 'They're all the same man — John Tesh.'
jokes.setup: The lineup features a musician, a journalist, and a sportscaster on Tuesday.
jokes.punchline: 'They're all the same man — John Tesh.' The joke is that John Tesh is a hack of all trades, none of them impressive.
jokes.explanation: A beautifully structured misdirect — the three-part list implies three impressive guests, then collapses into the single, deeply mediocre John Tesh. The economy is exceptional; the punchline is the name itself. The joke is entirely earned: John Tesh's Renaissance-man mediocrity was a known cultural target in the mid-'90s. Artie's deadpan sell makes it land.

jokes.text: Exchange about Jon Stewart going on 'before Larry' — 'That would be the news.'

jokes.punchline: Artie flatly notes: 'That would be the news.' Meaning: nothing precedes Larry — the absurdity of the suggestion is dismissed with one dry line.
jokes.explanation: Artie at his most economical — four words that shut down a conversation and land a laugh. The joke works on two levels: literal (Jon would be a news anchor) and dismissive (the idea is ludicrous). Strong character integration for Artie, the show's loyal institutional memory. Not groundbreaking, but perfectly executed.

jokes.explanation: A small but perfectly Artie moment — the sudden pivot to flattery as deflection is entirely in character for a man who navigates every room with a combination of bluster and charm. The awkwardness of 'I love those earrings' after a heated institutional discussion is the joke. Doesn't land huge, but it's precisely observed.

jokes.text: Larry's paranoid 'That's what they did to Johnny' speech about how Jay Leno replaced Carson via guest-hosting escalation.
jokes.setup: The network wants to build Jon Stewart a following via good guests.
jokes.punchline: Larry launches into a fully-formed, clearly well-rehearsed conspiracy theory about how Jay Leno supplanted Johnny Carson — which is both funny because it's paranoid AND because it's arguably accurate.
jokes.explanation: This is pure Larry Sanders comedy — character-driven paranoia that is simultaneously delusional AND perceptive. The real-world subtext (the actual Leno/Carson situation) gives the joke documentary weight. Only Larry Sanders would deliver this kind of insider-industry anxiety in a business meeting. The rewatch value is high because the show is literally about this very threat happening in real time to Larry.

jokes.setup: Costello explains why he's selling the car — he doesn't want to be a sad male menopause guy driving a sports car looking for sex.
jokes.punchline: He is selling the car to Hank, who has just explicitly said he wants it to get 'one third the pussy James Bond got.' The irony is perfect — he's handing the car directly to his cautionary tale.
jokes.explanation: This is the episode's first standout joke. The dramatic irony is perfectly constructed — the audience already knows WHY Hank bought the car (he just told us), so Costello's earnest self-congratulation about avoiding that exact cliché lands as a devastating callback. The structure is essentially a silent callback: Costello doesn't know he's talking to his cautionary tale. 'Nothing sadder' is the killer close. This earns its 8.5 because the joke is architecturally sophisticated — it requires holding two pieces of information simultaneously and the payoff is entirely earned, not cheap.

The character integration is nearly perfect; this is exactly the kind of thing only Hank would say and only Hank could make funny.

jokes.explanation: This is a sustained escalation sequence that works because each new excuse reveals more of Larry's narcissism. The Duchovny one is funny for foreshadowing reasons; the Margulies one ('she flirts with me') is the peak because it's simultaneously true (Larry uses on-air flirting) and pathetically ego-driven. Good character writing, though it runs a beat longer than ideal.

Each escalation is a beat, and the cumulative effect builds genuine discomfort that pays off across the entire episode. The structure is sophisticated: Duchovny's intentions are genuinely ambiguous, which makes it funnier. The joke earns its 8+ because it's the seed of the episode's most developed comedic thread, executed with perfect tonal ambiguity.

Randolph Scott (the classic Western actor widely rumored to have had a long relationship with Cary Grant) is an inspired reference — it's an insider Hollywood joke that rewards the knowledgeable viewer while being funny on its face even without the context. 'I've lost contact with that world' implies Artie was once plugged in, which opens a comic vista about his past without explaining it. The economy is perfect — it's one sentence doing the work of a whole subplot. Earns its 8.5+ because it's precisely the kind of layered, character-specific wit that defines this show at its best.

jokes.setup: Artie is presenting Jon Stewart's guest lineup as exciting.
jokes.punchline: He presents Charles Nelson Reilly as a 'hot' guest — a comedian primarily known from the 1970s game show circuit — and Jon's single-word response ('Again?') implies this has happened before.
jokes.explanation: A clean two-beat exchange. Artie's sincere delivery of 'the incomparable' for a minor celebrity combined with Jon's weary 'Again?' is a perfect illustration of the gap between what the show provides and what talent actually wants. Economy is strong.

dialogue.speaker: David Duchovny
dialogue.line: It's the kind of feeling That I normally have With a woman I like. It's like a warmth Or a buzz. It's definitely A heterosexual feeling, But it's directed At you. It's very Confusing to me.

jokes.text: The Duchovny gift — a leather jacket with 'The Truth Is Out There' on it — and the card reading 'For the beach and those cool—' before being interrupted by the 'Do you think he's gay?' question.
jokes.setup: Larry receives an expensive leather jacket from Duchovny with an X-Files reference on it.
jokes.punchline: The card begins reading as romantic ('for the beach and those cool—') and is interrupted at the most suggestive moment by Larry's paranoid question — the interruption IS the joke.
jokes.explanation: The interrupted card reading is a classic cringe comedy structure — the audience wants to hear the end of the card to assess whether it's romantic, but Larry derails the reading with the very question the card's ambiguity provokes. Smart construction.

dialogue.speaker: Elvis Costello
dialogue.line: With what you pay me, You're lucky You got the guitar.

jokes.text: Larry, when Artie asks if he 'did something to cause' Duchovny's crush: 'Yeah, look at me. I'm gorgeous. I'm just fucking gorgeous.'
jokes.setup: Artie asks whether Larry did something to encourage Duchovny's attention.
jokes.punchline: Larry responds with the most self-aggrandizing possible answer — delivered not as a joke but as sincere, paranoid narcissism. The absurdity of 'I'm just fucking gorgeous' as a complete explanation is the punchline.
jokes.explanation: A great Larry Sanders character moment — the answer is both absurd (he's not THAT gorgeous) and psychologically precise (Larry's narcissism is both his flaw and his comedic engine). 'I'm just fucking gorgeous' delivered without irony by Garry Shandling is the kind of line that defines the character.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: Oh, he's got a little Mad cow disease.

dialogue.speaker: Elvis Costello
dialogue.line: Ah, we'll keep him Out of england.

jokes.text: Larry asks Brian: 'Do I seem gay to you?' — Brian: 'That's hard to say, Larry, 'cause I know you're not gay, right?'
jokes.setup: Larry, consumed by the Duchovny situation, asks his straight male colleague for a gay assessment.
jokes.punchline: Brian's response is both an endorsement and a hedge — 'I know you're not gay, right?' checking for confirmation of something he's suddenly not sure about.
jokes.explanation: A solid cringe beat — Brian's uncertain 'right?' after declaring Larry straight introduces doubt that is both socially awkward and funny. The conversation is going to an uncomfortable place and the actors are navigating it with precision.

dialogue.speaker: Network Executive
dialogue.line: I have seen that Three times.

jokes.text: Brian: 'I don't think [my gay friends] think about sex when they watch you. Really, but I haven't exactly taken a survey.'
jokes.setup: Larry asks if Brian's gay friends think he's gay.
jokes.punchline: Brian offers the backhanded reassurance that gay men don't find Larry sexually interesting — then undermines it with 'I haven't taken a survey,' implying there might be data that says otherwise.
jokes.explanation: A neat two-beat joke — the initial reassurance is itself insulting (gay men don't sexualize Larry), and the caveat opens the wound back up. Functional cringe comedy.

dialogue.speaker: David Duchovny
dialogue.line: God, you really care About me, don't you?

dialogue.speaker: David Duchovny
dialogue.line: Are you uncomfortable?

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: A little bit.

jokes.text: Larry: 'Do any of your friends think I'm gay?' / 'My gay friends?' / 'OK, sure. Let's start with them.'
jokes.setup: Larry wants to know if his friends perceive him as gay
jokes.punchline: Brian's clarifying question assumes Larry means his gay friends specifically — and Larry immediately accepts this as a reasonable starting population for the survey
jokes.explanation: A beautifully efficient three-line exchange. Brian's instinctive segmentation of his friends by sexuality, and Larry's immediate acceptance of the subsample without any acknowledgment of how strange this is, generates a dry, sophisticated laugh.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: You know, you talk To people on television, Next thing, They think that you're Their new best friend.

jokes.text: Brian on Duchovny: 'A third think he's gay, a third think he's bi, and the rest don't care. They just want to kiss him anyways, which would be me.'
jokes.setup: Larry asks Brian whether Duchovny seems gay.
jokes.punchline: Brian's breakdown of his gay friends' opinions on Duchovny culminates in the reveal that Brian himself wants to kiss Duchovny — delivered as a casual, matter-of-fact admission.
jokes.explanation: The surprise pivot at the end — 'which would be me' — is a perfectly placed twist. The three-part breakdown (gay/bi/don't care) is a classic setup that puts the audience on guard, but the personal revelation lands unexpectedly. The casual delivery is everything. Strong structure.

jokes.text: Brian, upon hearing the security guard is looking for him: 'The gorgeous security guard? Get over here! I'm in trouble, and I love it.'
jokes.setup: Someone mentions the security guard is looking for Brian.
jokes.punchline: Brian immediately establishes the security guard as gorgeous and embraces the idea of being 'in trouble' with evident pleasure — a quick character moment that extends the Brian-sexuality running thread.
jokes.explanation: A quick character button that extends Brian's emerging queer characterization in a light, charming way. 'I'm in trouble, and I love it' is a nice line. Works as a running gag beat.

jokes.text: Hank's muffler mechanic confrontation: '$300 for a water pump? Hank! But I still smell gas. Hank! Yes! I do realize that the water pump is not connected to the fuel system, but I just had the mistaken impression that you had a nose. Tally ho, fuck face!'
jokes.setup: Hank is arguing with a mechanic about the car repairs.
jokes.punchline: 'Tally ho, fuck face!' — Hank's exit line that combines a mock-British aristocratic farewell with a blunt profanity, a perfect distillation of his pretension and rage.
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's most quotable and character-perfect moments. 'Tally ho, fuck face' is a genuinely inspired juxtaposition — the posh British hunting call immediately followed by crude American profanity. It could only come from Hank, a man who aspires to elegance and habitually falls into vulgarity. The line is also structurally preceded by Hank making a legitimate mechanical point ('the water pump is not connected to the fuel system') which shows intelligence, before the explosive exit demolishes the pretense. Strong earns-vs-cheap score because this is character-specific comedy, not a cheap shock.

jokes.text: The car fire: 'Your car's on fire.' Hank explodes — 'God damn it! When were you gonna tell me?!'
jokes.setup: In the middle of a conversation, someone calmly informs Hank that his car is on fire.
jokes.punchline: The casual delivery of 'your car's on fire' is the joke — and Hank's explosion of 'When were you gonna tell me?!' implies there was a significant delay in reporting this fire.
jokes.explanation: The perfect escalation endpoint for the Jensen Healey storyline. The entire car arc (purchase → mechanical failures → gas smell → fire) has been building to this. 'When were you gonna tell me?!' implies someone stood and watched the car burn before mentioning it, which adds an absurdist layer. The callback payoff is maximally satisfying.

jokes.text: Writers' room: 'We can still call it Welcome to the White House. Not that Hank in a wig isn't funny. Just it's a little mean.'
jokes.setup: Writers are reworking the sketch after Jon Stewart's criticism.
jokes.punchline: 'Not that Hank in a wig isn't funny' — an aside that confirms they've already tried this gag and it works, but is being cut for being too mean. The meta-acknowledgment of a gag we haven't seen is itself a gag.
jokes.explanation: A meta-moment that rewards regular viewers of the show who know Hank well enough to immediately picture the wig gag. The aside is charming and industry-specific.

jokes.text: Jon's guest week summary: 'I'm gonna talk to Brent Musburger about ABC, then talk to Zsa Zsa Gabor about Brent Musburger, then just ride that crest right into Charles Nelson Reilly. Then I'm gonna hang myself with my own shoelaces.'
jokes.setup: Jon is reviewing his guest lineup.
jokes.punchline: 'Then I'm gonna hang myself with my own shoelaces' — the jokey threat of self-harm as the logical conclusion of this guest booking is the dark button.
jokes.explanation: A nicely structured escalation — riding the guests' names like a toboggan toward the cliff edge of 'hang myself with my own shoelaces.' The callback to the terrible guest lineup pays off. Jon playing a version of himself griping about being saddled with bad guests adds a meta layer.

jokes.text: Jon about Hootie: 'Hootie seems aloof.'
jokes.setup: Larry asks if Jon is friends with the Blowfish.
jokes.punchline: Jon's assessment of Hootie Darius Rucker as 'aloof' is a perfectly dry character observation — distinguishing between the bandmates with mock-sociological precision.
jokes.explanation: Three words that do everything. 'Hootie seems aloof' as a sincere characterization of a mid-90s pop star is absurdly specific and funny. Maximum economy. The joke is in the mock-earnestness of the social assessment.

jokes.text: Jon to Larry: 'You wouldn't happen to be friends with Sally Struthers, would you?'
jokes.setup: Larry has been revealing that all his objections to giving Jon his guests are about personal relationships.
jokes.punchline: Jon suggests Sally Struthers as a guest — but the implication is that she's an even more embarrassing booking than Charles Nelson Reilly, delivered as if it would be a relief.
jokes.explanation: A clean industry-insider joke — Sally Struthers (a beloved but faded '70s celebrity) as a 'desirable' guest is funny for the same reason Charles Nelson Reilly is. Jon's resigned tone makes it land.

jokes.text: Jon: 'Normally, I would do this behind your back, but, you know, you're a good guy.'
jokes.setup: Jon is discussing the process of guest negotiations openly with Larry.
jokes.punchline: Jon casually admits that the standard practice is to do exactly this kind of maneuvering behind people's backs — and treats his transparency as a personal courtesy.
jokes.explanation: A sharply observed industry-politics moment — the casual admission that everyone operates with hidden agendas, framed as a favor not to. Jon's honesty about dishonesty is the joke. Clean and economical.

jokes.text: The Duchovny guest-stealing argument: 'Why'd you steal Duchovny from me?' 'Get off it. You stole Duchovny. I just took him back.' 'Well, I had to throw Jon a bone.'
jokes.setup: Larry confronts Artie about moving Duchovny to Jon's show.
jokes.punchline: 'You stole Duchovny. I just took him back' — Artie's logic reframes his own theft as repossession. 'Throw Jon a bone' trivializes giving Duchovny (whom Larry obsesses over) as a minor favor.
jokes.explanation: A solid exchange that works because of all the Duchovny context built up — treating a celebrity as property to be traded and re-traded while Larry clearly has non-professional feelings about him is the irony. Artie's casual justification is perfectly in character.

jokes.text: Artie: 'Besides, you said Duchovny's making goo-goo eyes at you. I thought I was doing you a favor.' Larry: 'Why don't you just let me worry about his little goo-goo eyes?'
jokes.setup: Artie justifies moving Duchovny to Jon's show.
jokes.punchline: Larry's defensive 'why don't you just let me worry about his little goo-goo eyes' — asserting ownership over someone's romantic attention for him — is absurd and revealing simultaneously.
jokes.explanation: 'Let me worry about his little goo-goo eyes' is a delicious line — the possessive framing of someone else's crush as Larry's personal domain. The word 'little' adds a condescending softness. Strong character integration.

jokes.text: Larry's accusation: 'You're just trying to get in good with Jon Stewart so that when he pushes me out, you'll have a job.'
jokes.setup: Larry escalates the Artie confrontation to existential paranoia.
jokes.punchline: The accusation is both paranoid AND not entirely wrong — the entire episode has been about this threat. Larry's neurotic self-awareness exists on the same frequency as his obliviousness.
jokes.explanation: This is where Larry's comedy and tragedy merge — the paranoia is so specific and yet so plausible that it stops being entirely funny and starts being painfully true. Character integration is near-perfect. Rewatch value because this is the emotional spine of the season.

jokes.text: Artie: 'You don't know what the fuck you're talking about.' Larry: 'Fuck I don't.'
jokes.setup: Larry accuses Artie of betrayal.
jokes.punchline: 'Fuck I don't' — a grammatically odd but perfectly comprehensible affirmation ('The fuck I don't' = 'I most certainly do know'). The exchange is brief, heated, and funny for its bluntness.
jokes.explanation: The exchange has the rhythm of a real argument, and 'Fuck I don't' is an authentic piece of dialogue. Functional character comedy without being remarkable.

jokes.text: Assistant interrupts the heated argument: 'Excuse me, Larry. David Duchovny's on line 2.' Artie: 'Oh, Larry, your girlfriend's on the phone. You better hurry. He's in a good mood today.'
jokes.setup: Larry and Artie are in a tense, genuine argument about professional betrayal.
jokes.punchline: Artie defuses his own anger by calling Duchovny Larry's 'girlfriend' — the cruelest possible word choice given Larry's anxiety about Duchovny's sexuality.
jokes.explanation: Artie's 'your girlfriend's on the phone' is a precision weapon — it hits Larry's deepest anxiety (that he might be gay or perceived as gay) while simultaneously reducing a big fight to nothing. The casual 'He's in a good mood today' is a perfect button. Strong character integration and excellent economy.

jokes.text: During Elvis Costello's performance, someone is visibly mocking him: 'What are you doing?' 'I'm mocking him because he's an asshole.'
jokes.setup: Elvis Costello performs an emotional, serious ballad on the show.
jokes.punchline: During the performance, Hank (or a staff member) is caught silently mocking Costello — and when asked, provides the bluntest possible justification.
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's most perfectly timed lines — it drops during a serious musical performance like a bomb. 'I'm mocking him because he's an asshole' is both honest and hilarious, and it completely recontextualizes everything happening onscreen. The economy is outstanding. The callback to the Jensen Healey disaster makes it land much harder. Earns its 8+ for the combination of timing, economy, and contextual richness.

jokes.text: After the performance, backstage: Hank confronts Costello about the car. Costello: 'It's not a car. It's a driving machine.'
jokes.setup: Hank tells Costello that the car caught fire and is leaking gasoline.
jokes.punchline: Costello's response — 'It's not a car, it's a driving machine' — is a pure salesman's deflection, pivoting from the safety concern to a brand-speak non-answer.
jokes.explanation: Costello's pivot to promotional language for a burning vehicle is perfect — 'driving machine' as the euphemism for 'explosive liability.' It also echoes his earlier romantic description of the car while dropping it.

jokes.text: Hank: 'Man, I should've learned my lesson when I bought that moped from Sting. There's your problem. You don't buy anything from Sting.'
jokes.setup: Hank is confronting Elvis Costello about the defective car.
jokes.punchline: Hank reveals he has a prior history of buying vehicles from British rock stars — specifically a bad moped from Sting — and draws the lesson that you shouldn't buy anything from ANY of them.
jokes.explanation: A genuinely inspired comedy beat. The suggestion that Hank has an established pattern of buying vehicles from British rock stars — and has learned nothing from the Sting moped incident — is absurdist character comedy at its finest. The specificity (moped, Sting) elevates it beyond a generic celebrity joke. 'You don't buy anything from Sting' as a life maxim is instantly quotable and reveals a whole comic history we never see. This earns its 8.5 because it's original, character-specific, economical, and earns every laugh through genuine wit.

jokes.text: Hank: 'Oh, save it for your Limey bullshit love songs, will you, please? You owe me money, asshole.'
jokes.setup: Costello tries to defend the car.
jokes.punchline: Hank dismisses Costello's artistic credibility as 'Limey bullshit love songs' — a deeply philistine assessment of one of rock's most critically respected artists — then pivots to the money owed.
jokes.explanation: 'Limey bullshit love songs' is a perfect Hank construction — contemptuous, specific, and wrong (Costello is far more than a love-song artist). The pivot to 'you owe me money, asshole' is a clean escalation. Strong character integration.

jokes.text: The director calls '5 seconds' and Hank has to immediately pivot from furious confrontation to a cheerful on-air persona — then sighs and walks out smiling.
jokes.setup: Hank is in the middle of a heated argument with Costello when the director calls the countdown.
jokes.punchline: The professionalism of television — Hank must instantly become the cheerful sidekick — is visually embodied in the sigh-and-smile pivot. The gap between inner rage and on-air persona is the show's core irony, compressed into a single moment.
jokes.explanation: A visual/structural joke rather than a verbal one — the show-must-go-on moment is a Larry Sanders signature. The sigh into the smile encapsulates Hank's entire character: all private chaos, all public performativity. Earns its craft score for how much it achieves without words.

jokes.text: Back on air, Costello says it's 'always nice to be back' — then backstage: 'With what you pay me, you're lucky you got the guitar.'
jokes.setup: Costello's on-air persona is warm and gracious ('always nice to be back').
jokes.punchline: Backstage, he immediately reveals he's annoyed about pay — complaining that his full band isn't there because of the show's low fee.
jokes.explanation: A clean public/private contrast — the show's essential joke applied to a guest. 'You're lucky you got the guitar' is a nicely specific complaint. The fact that it comes from Costello, who has just caused Hank's car to catch fire, adds an extra irony layer.

jokes.text: Larry's monologue sign-off guest list: 'I want to thank P.J. O'Rourke, comedian Kip Addotta, and of course Elvis Costello. And we'll see you all tomorrow night... Jon Stewart will be guest hosting. And uh, you may now flip.'
jokes.setup: Standard late-night sign-off
jokes.punchline: 'You may now flip' — Larry's signature sign-off ('No flipping' to keep viewers during commercial, now 'you may now flip' at the end) combined with the passively bitter mention of Jon Stewart as guest host creates a funny tonal shift
jokes.explanation: The 'No flipping/you may now flip' bit is a meta running gag within the show-within-the-show, and this deployment at the end of an episode where Larry is insecure about Jon Stewart gives it an ironic undertone.

jokes.text: Larry confronts Duchovny about his apparent attraction: 'Clearly, you — and I support it completely — are gay, and I'm straight.' Duchovny: 'I'm not gay. I'm also straight.'
jokes.setup: Larry works up the nerve to confront Duchovny about what he perceives as a gay crush.
jokes.punchline: Duchovny's flat denial — 'I'm not gay. I'm also straight' — delivered with no offense taken, is hilarious in its complete normalcy against Larry's elaborate anxiety.
jokes.explanation: The payoff to the episode's central comedic engine. Larry's careful, diplomatic delivery of 'and I support it completely — are gay' is a masterpiece of tortured political correctness, and Duchovny's utterly calm 'I'm not gay. I'm also straight.' demolishes the structure Larry has been building all episode. The repeated confirmation ('I'm not gay. I'm ALSO straight') implies Larry isn't convinced by the first denial. Strong character integration — only Larry could turn this into such an elaborate, anxious construction.

jokes.text: Duchovny: 'That's OK. I'm not — I'm not gay. I'm — I'm also straight.'
jokes.setup: Larry has formally rejected Duchovny's supposed advances, citing Duchovny's supposed homosexuality
jokes.punchline: Duchovny calmly clarifies that he's not gay, deflating the entire elaborate construction Larry has built — but the phrasing 'I'm also straight' is slightly odd, suggesting this is not quite a complete denial
jokes.explanation: 'I'm also straight' is a perfect construction — the 'also' implies he's agreeing with Larry's 'I'm straight' while simultaneously being just ambiguous enough to keep the viewer uncertain. It deflates Larry's elaborate preparation while not entirely resolving the question. Very well-structured beat.

jokes.text: Duchovny describes his heterosexual feelings for Larry: 'It's the kind of feeling I normally have with a woman I like. It's like a warmth or a buzz. It's definitely a heterosexual feeling, but it's directed at you. It's very confusing to me.'
jokes.setup: Duchovny explains that he isn't gay but still finds Larry attractive.
jokes.punchline: Duchovny's earnest, analytical deconstruction of his own feelings — 'a warmth or a buzz,' 'heterosexual feeling but directed at you' — is so sincerely confused that it's both funny and genuinely uncomfortable.
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's most distinctive comedy moments — Duchovny's earnest phenomenology of his confused hetero-attraction to Larry is both deeply funny and surprisingly moving. The joke is that Duchovny is being completely sincere and analytical about something that is inherently absurd, and his sincerity makes Larry more uncomfortable than any outright declaration could. 'A warmth or a buzz' applied to Larry Sanders is inspired. Earns its 8.5 for originality and the genuine commitment to the comedic premise.

jokes.text: Larry: 'I'm a little uncomfortable.' Duchovny: 'Oh god, 6:30. I gotta run.'
jokes.setup: Duchovny has just delivered an intimate speech about his heterosexual feelings for Larry.
jokes.punchline: Duchovny instantly and completely pivots from profound emotional intimacy to 'I gotta run' — the speed of the deflation is the joke.
jokes.explanation: A perfect comedy structure — build to the most uncomfortable possible moment, then deflate instantly. Duchovny's time-check is the funniest possible exit from the most intimate conversation in the episode. The economy of 'Oh god, 6:30. I gotta run.' against the weight of what preceded it is exceptional. Earns its 8+ for the structural precision.

jokes.text: Network exec Roger's lineup critique — runs through the terrible Jon Stewart guest list and then reveals: 'And Joan Embry. Well, Joan's bringing in a 20-foot snake and some wonderful footage of a cow giving birth to a rare albino calf. I have seen that three times.'
jokes.setup: Roger complains about the weak Jon Stewart guest lineup.
jokes.punchline: The final guest booking is Joan Embry with a snake and cow-birth footage — and Roger's weary 'I have seen that three times' is the button.
jokes.explanation: The escalating badness of the guest lineup (Zsa Zsa → Charles Nelson Reilly → Jamie Farr → Joan Embry with a 20-foot snake) is a sustained escalation joke. 'I have seen that three times' is perfect deadpan exhaustion. The cow-birth footage adds an absurdist peak.

jokes.text: Duchovny appears on the lot, introduces 'Carol' — a woman — and asks for 'just a minute' alone with Larry.
jokes.setup: Artie has told the exec he's 'about to make him very happy' — implying he booked a major guest. Then Duchovny appears.
jokes.punchline: The reveal that Artie's ace was getting Duchovny back for Jon Stewart's show — by engineering the situation so Duchovny naturally moves himself
jokes.explanation: The structural comedy of the scene — Artie's confident 'I'm about to make you happy' followed by the reveal of his scheme — works as plot comedy more than joke comedy. The payoff is more satisfying than funny.

jokes.text: Network exec's Jon Stewart guest lineup critique — Sally Struthers ('funny'), Zsa Zsa Gabor ('she's hot'), Charles Nelson Reilly ('hilarious'), Jamie Farr, Joan Embry — then: 'I have seen that [albino calf birth footage] three times.'
jokes.setup: Network exec complains about Jon Stewart's weak guest lineup
jokes.punchline: Each 'guest' is worse than the last, culminating in Joan Embry bringing zoo animals and footage of a cow giving birth — which the exec has apparently seen so many times on this show that he's lost count
jokes.explanation: The cumulative guest-lineup joke reaches its nadir with Joan Embry and the albino calf birth footage, which the exec has seen 'three times.' This is the final payoff of the running gag about the quality difference between Larry's show and what Jon Stewart is being offered. 'I have seen that three times' is very funny in its weary specificity.

jokes.text: Duchovny introduces Carol: 'This is the friend who I was visiting on the lot yesterday.' Artie brings her in just as the exec says he's 'about to make you very happy.'
jokes.setup: The exec has promised to make Larry happy; Artie then brings someone in — the viewer expects a star guest
jokes.punchline: The 'good news' turns out to be Duchovny... with a girlfriend, completely defusing the previous episode's sexual tension and the exec's promised solution simultaneously
jokes.explanation: The structural comedy here is solid — the 'good news' delivery is subverted by the completely mundane arrival of Duchovny with a girlfriend. The joke works on multiple levels: it resolves the gay question (sort of), it trivializes the exec's promise, and it sets up the final twist.

jokes.text: After Duchovny pretends to be upset that he's being moved to Jon Stewart's show (due to Artie's secret machinations), he breaks: 'God, you really care about me, don't you?'
jokes.setup: Larry is visibly angry that Duchovny has been moved to Jon's show (actually, because Artie moved him — but Duchovny doesn't know Larry did it).
jokes.punchline: Duchovny reads Larry's fury as proof of emotional attachment — 'you really care about me' — which is both accidentally correct (Larry does care, but about the guest booking politics) and a reactivation of the gay-crush misread.
jokes.explanation: A beautifully constructed irony — Duchovny reads the wrong emotion (professional frustration) as the right one (personal care). The dramatic irony is rich because the audience knows multiple truths simultaneously: Larry IS upset (but about booking), and he DOES find Duchovny's attention flattering. The layer on layer makes this a standout moment.

jokes.text: Duchovny: 'Are you uncomfortable?' Larry: 'A little bit.' Duchovny: 'Okay, I'll see you.'
jokes.setup: Duchovny has just expressed that Larry's anger proves he cares.
jokes.punchline: The breezy 'Okay, I'll see you' after Larry's admission of discomfort — Duchovny again simply exits the emotional high point — mirrors the earlier '6:30' deflation and establishes it as his character's comic signature.
jokes.explanation: The second instance of the Duchovny deflation pattern — now established as a running gag. The joke has more context and the structural echo makes it funnier on rewatch. Economy is near-perfect: three words ('Okay, I'll see you') dispatch the entire emotional scene.

jokes.text: Artie's coda: 'Next time, kick him in the balls.'
jokes.setup: Larry emerges from the Duchovny encounter and asks if he looked angry.
jokes.punchline: Artie's advice for managing unwanted emotional attention from a man: 'Next time, kick him in the balls.' Delivered with total practicality, as if this is obvious crisis management.
jokes.explanation: A perfect Artie line — blunt, practical, and entirely in character for a man who solves everything with directness. The advice is so simple and physical against the elaborate emotional texture of the Duchovny subplot that it lands like a release valve. Quotability is very high. Only Artie could say this in exactly this way.

jokes.text: Artie's summary advice after Duchovny leaves: 'It's my job to protect the host from people like that.'
jokes.setup: Larry is processing the entire Duchovny experience
jokes.punchline: Artie's self-description of his role — protecting Larry from genuine human connections while engineering fake ones — framed as professional responsibility
jokes.explanation: A quietly devastating observation about the entertainment industry — Artie's job is to insulate Larry from reality, including the reality of a person who genuinely likes him. The comedy is dark and the line contains the show's entire thesis about celebrity and connection.

jokes.text: Artie's observation about television friendship: 'You know, you talk to people on television, next thing, they think you're their new best friend.' Larry: 'Well, he IS a friend of mine, you know.' Artie: 'Well, go with me on this.'
jokes.setup: Artie frames the Duchovny situation as a case of parasocial parasitism.
jokes.punchline: Larry corrects Artie — Duchovny actually IS his friend — and Artie's response ('Well, go with me on this') reveals he's just using a convenient narrative that lets him protect Larry while preserving his own power.
jokes.explanation: 'Well, go with me on this' is a beautifully crafted line — Artie is caught in a convenient fiction and simply asks Larry to participate in it. It's both a practical TV-world observation AND a perfect Artie character moment, managing perceptions as always. The line lands because of Rip Torn's delivery and the accumulated context.

jokes.text: The closing scene: Charlie (Charles Nelson Reilly, apparently) arrives looking for Jon Stewart to 'have a drink and talk' — completely unaware of his place in the show's comedic hierarchy.
jokes.setup: Charles Nelson Reilly arrives at the studio.
jokes.punchline: After being the butt of every terrible-guest-lineup joke all episode, CNR shows up in person — cheerful, eager, wanting to socialize with Jon Stewart. The irony is that he has no idea he's a punchline.
jokes.explanation: A strong structural callback — the character who has been the punchline of guest-booking jokes all episode arrives in the flesh, oblivious. The joke is entirely situational and works best for viewers who tracked the CNR references throughout. Rewatch value is high because knowing this is coming makes the earlier jokes funnier.

tmdb_overview: Larry, worried about the implications of a permanent guest host, sabotages temporary host Jon Stewart at every turn. Hank buys a less-than-perfect used car from Elvis Costello. David Duchovny's friendliness makes Larry wonder about his sexual orientation.
